transcript.text: Hi, I'm Sensei. Put your page under the camera and start solving. I'm watching.
You changed the subscript in H2O to make H2O2—what substance is that, and is it still water?
It's still water, just with two oxygens. And it balances, two H and two O on each side.
Okay, let me think.
It's not water—it's hydrogen peroxide. Water is H2O. Try balancing the original equation again.
Okay but the atoms are balanced though. Why does it matter what it's called?
Good question. One moment.
It matters because H2O2 is a different substance with different properties, even if the atoms balance.
Hmm okay, so I can't change the little numbers. Then how do I balance it?
Let me see.
You're right, you can't change the little numbers. Let's find a way to balance it without changing them.
Yeah but how? If I keep H2O there's only one O on the right.
Got it. Give me a second.
You're right, H2O has only one oxygen on the right. Let's find a way to fix that without changing the formula.
You keep saying that. Like what way? Do I put a number in front or something?
Okay, let me think.
You can't change the formula. Try putting a number in front of H2O instead.
So H2 plus O2 gives 2 H2O? Now there's two O each side but four H on the right.
Good question. One moment.
You're on the right track—now check how many hydrogen atoms are on each side.
Two on the left, four on the right. So 2 H2 plus O2 gives 2 H2O. That's balanced.
Let me see.
You're close—now check how many oxygen atoms are on each side.
Two O each side, four H each side. Done, 2 H2 plus O2 to 2 H2O. Thanks.
Got it. Give me a second.
You've got it—2 H2 plus O2 gives 2 H2O, and it's balanced. Great job!
